description: Somos un equipo de apasionados por la astronomía, la ciencia, la programación y el arte. Nuestra esencia nace de la curiosidad por comprender el universo y de la necesidad de crear dentro de él. Combinamos el pensamiento lógico de la programación, la fascinación por el cosmos y la sensibilidad del arte para experimentar, aprender y construir juntos.
summary:
NASA Terra Tones is a web-based jukebox that turns NASA's scientific visualizations of Earth into music, so blind and low-vision people can explore the same data shown at the Earth Information Center. It is a project by team Dark Nebula for the NASA Space Apps challenge The Earth Information Jukebox.

Each NASA image is analyzed in the browser and converted into sound. Brightness becomes pitch, color becomes timbre, texture becomes rhythm and position becomes stereo, while unusual areas ring a bell. Users can play an image like a score or explore it cell by cell with the keyboard, guided by text descriptions and narration. The interface aims for WCAG 2.2 AA and works with screen readers. By giving Earth data a voice, the project makes climate and environmental science more inclusive.
details:
NASA Terra Tones is a web-based "jukebox" that converts NASA’s scientific visualizations of Earth into music, allowing blind or low-vision individuals to explore the same data that others see on screen. Each image—covering topics such as sea temperature, Arctic ice, ocean color, vegetation, or global precipitation—is divided into a 16×9 grid and analyzed directly within the browser. The brightness of each cell determines the pitch of a note on a pentatonic scale; the color dictates the timbre, saturation controls the volume, texture influences the rhythm, and the cell’s location determines its position within the stereo field. Unusual areas are highlighted by the sound of a bell, while the image's contrast sets the tempo. Users can listen to the image as a musical score—playing from left to right—or navigate through it cell by cell using a keyboard. Additionally, each cell includes a text description, and a voice-over provides a summary of the image.

The project offers several benefits: it provides non-visual access to data that is currently almost exclusively visual; it offers an intuitive way to perceive patterns—such as warm or cold zones, contrasts, and anomalies—and serves as an educational tool that functions in any web browser without the need for installation. We hope it will be used in classrooms, museums, and spaces like the Earth Information Center, and that it will inspire the release of more Earth-related data in an audible format.

The project is built using JavaScript—incorporating ES modules, Vite, the Canvas API, D3.js, Tone.js, the Web Speech API, and the NASA Scientific Visualization Studio (SVS)—along with a Node.js script for downloading images and "axe-core" for accessibility audits. It requires no special server or hardware; a computer or mobile device with a web browser is all that is needed.
